questions.q: Why can a contract end up at different addresses on different chains when deployed with plain `CREATE`?
options: Because Solidity compiles differently per chain
Because CREATE derives the address from the deployer's address and its transaction nonce, which diverges across chains as transaction history differs
Because each chain has a different EVM version always
Because gas prices differ per chain
questions.explain: CREATE's address depends on the deployer's nonce at deploy time — once nonces diverge even slightly across chains, the same deployer gets a different address on each.

questions.q: What does `CREATE2` derive a contract's address from, instead of the deployer's nonce?
options: The current block timestamp
The deployer's address, a salt, and the contract's init code
The gas price at deployment
A random number generated by the EVM
questions.explain: CREATE2's address formula uses deployer + salt + init code hash — none of which depend on transaction history, so the same inputs on different chains produce the same address.

questions.q: What does a GitHub Actions `strategy.matrix` block let a multi-chain deploy workflow do?
options: Deploy to only one chain at a time, sequentially, with manual approval between each
Run the same job once per list entry (e.g. per network), in parallel, each as its own isolated job
Automatically generate a CREATE2 salt
Replace the need for a --rpc-url flag entirely
questions.explain: strategy.matrix runs one job instance per entry in the list — here, one deploy job per target network, in parallel, isolated from each other.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why doesn't multisig discipline (Lesson 16) collapse into a single approval covering all chains?
options: Because multisig only works on Ethereum mainnet
Because each chain's deployment transaction needs its own confirmations from that chain's own Safe — a 5-chain deploy means 5 separate confirmation flows
Because Safe accounts can't be deployed on testnets
Because CREATE2 makes multisig unnecessary
questions.explain: A Safe is deployed and operates per chain, so each chain's deployment transaction requires its own round of confirmations — multisig discipline has to be repeated, not done once.

questions.q: What is a "deterministic deployment proxy," as described in this lesson?
options: A tool that hides a contract's source code
A shared, well-known factory contract already deployed at the same address on most EVM chains, used so CREATE2 addresses stay consistent without custom tooling
A type of multisig wallet
A GitHub Actions runner specifically for deployments
questions.explain: Rather than every team building its own CREATE2 factory, most rely on a shared deterministic deployment proxy already present at a consistent address across chains.
